items.title: Reading a meniscus from the wrong angle changes the answer
items.claim: Read a burette with your eye above the meniscus: you see a high reading. Read with your eye below: a low reading. The error can be several percent — purely from where you put your head.
items.prompt: What's the right way to take the reading?

options.text: Eye level with the meniscus, viewing perpendicular to the scale, so the line of sight passes through the bottom of the meniscus and the scale at the same level
From slightly above to see the bottom of the meniscus better
From below to avoid disturbing the liquid

items.reveal:
Parallax error happens when the object you are reading and the scale you are reading against are at different distances from your eye. Any tilt in viewing angle shifts the apparent position of one relative to the other.

For a meniscus in a burette: the liquid surface and the scale on the burette tube are separated by a few millimetres. Looking down or up at an angle moves them apparently relative to each other.

Same problem with ammeters and voltmeters with mirror scales: align your eye so the needle and its reflection in the mirror coincide. This way you know you're looking perpendicular.

Digital readouts eliminate parallax (the reading is a single number). They introduce other concerns: rounding, response time, calibration drift.
items.why: Lab errors are taught as 'be careful'. Parallax is a specific systematic error with a specific fix — eye level, perpendicular sighting.

items.title: Two particles agree faster than light can travel
items.claim: Prepare two entangled photons and send them light-years apart. Measure the polarisation of one. The other's polarisation is instantly determined — apparently faster than light could send a signal between them.
items.prompt: Does this violate special relativity (no information faster than c)?

options.text: No — the correlations are perfect but the local result is random; you cannot send information until classical comparison is made
No — entangled particles communicate through a third dimension

items.reveal_title: Bell's theorem ruled out local hidden variables
items.reveal:
Einstein, Podolsky and Rosen in 1935 argued that quantum mechanics must be incomplete: there must be 'hidden variables' that determine outcomes locally, and entanglement just looks spooky because we don't see those variables.

In 1964 John Bell showed any local hidden-variable theory must satisfy a mathematical inequality. Real entangled particles VIOLATE this inequality. Experimental tests (Aspect 1982, and many since, culminating in 'loophole-free' tests by 2015) confirmed quantum mechanics over local realism.

But quantum correlations cannot be used for signalling: Alice's local measurement looks random no matter what Bob does, until they compare classically. The 2022 Nobel Prize honoured Clauser, Aspect and Zeilinger for this work.
items.why: Classical intuitions about pre-existing properties and local causes fail. Quantum systems can be entangled in ways with no classical analogue.

items.title: Pitch, loudness and timbre are three independent properties of a sound
items.claim: A piano middle C and a flute middle C have the same pitch (frequency around 262 Hz). They sound completely different. A whisper and a shout at middle C have the same pitch but different loudness. Three independent dimensions describe a musical tone.
items.prompt: What's the physical basis of each?

options.text: All three are different combinations of frequency
Pitch corresponds to fundamental frequency; loudness corresponds to wave amplitude (intensity); timbre corresponds to the specific mixture of harmonics (overtones) above the fundamental
Pitch and loudness are the same physical quantity
Timbre is an illusion of the ear

items.reveal:
When a piano string vibrates at 262 Hz (middle C), it actually produces a complex waveform: a fundamental at 262 Hz plus harmonics at 524, 786, 1048 Hz etc. The relative strengths of those harmonics — and how they decay over time — give the piano its characteristic 'sound'.

A flute at the same note has very different harmonic content: stronger odd harmonics, less attack noise. A trumpet has yet another mix. The Fourier spectrum of a 'middle C' is a fingerprint of the instrument.

Loudness is approximately log of intensity. Decibel scale: 10 × log10(I/I0), where I0 is the threshold of hearing (about 10 to the minus 12 W/m²). A whisper is around 30 dB; conversational speech 60 dB; rock concert 120 dB. A 10 dB increase is about a doubling of perceived loudness.
items.why: Sound is often treated as 'a wave with a pitch'. It has three (and arguably more) independent properties that the ear perceives separately.
